nameStory: The eastern cottontail gets its charming name from its fluffy white tail that looks exactly like a cotton ball when it's raised in alarm. When these rabbits hop away from danger, that bright white 'cotton' tail bobs up and down like a warning flag. The 'eastern' part simply tells us this is the cottontail species most common in the eastern United States.
description: The eastern cottontail is New England's most common rabbit, about the size of a small house cat with long ears and powerful hind legs. These brownish-gray rabbits have that famous white cotton-ball tail and typically weigh 2-3 pounds when fully grown. You'll recognize them by their alert posture, large dark eyes, and tendency to freeze motionless when they sense danger before suddenly bounding away in zigzag patterns. They're most active during dawn and dusk hours when they venture out to feed on grasses and plants.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: About the size of a small house cat with a compact, rounded body and disproportionately large hind legs that look built for jumping. Ears are long and upright, roughly 2-3 inches tall, and constantly swiveling to catch sounds.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Soft, dense fur that's brownish-gray on top with a lighter, almost white belly. The fur has a grizzled appearance up close with individual hairs banded in different colors - dark at the tips, lighter in the middle.

idTips.label: Tail
idTips.description: The unmistakable white, fluffy tail that looks like a cotton ball - bright white underneath and clearly visible when raised. About 2 inches long and stands out dramatically against the brown body.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Four-print hopping pattern with large oval hind prints (about 3 inches) landing ahead of smaller round front prints. Look for the distinctive Y-shaped imprint of the hind feet in soft mud or snow.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Freezes completely motionless when alarmed, then suddenly bolts in a zigzag pattern with powerful leaps. Most active at dawn and dusk, often seen sitting statue-still in open areas before bounding to cover.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Look for small, round, marble-sized droppings that are dry and fibrous. Also watch for clean 45-degree angle cuts on twigs and stems where they've been gnawing, and shallow depressions in grass where they rest.

habitat: Eastern cottontails thrive in edge habitats where open areas meet brushy cover - think field edges, suburban yards, parks, and meadows bordered by shrubs or woods. They love areas with a mix of grasses for feeding and dense vegetation for quick escape, making them perfectly adapted to human-modified landscapes. You'll often spot them in cemetery grounds, golf courses, and backyard gardens where they can dash between lawn areas and ornamental plantings.

seasonality.spring: Most active season as breeding begins and fresh green vegetation emerges. Look for adults with noticeably worn fur from winter, and by late spring, watch for tiny young rabbits barely larger than hamsters.
seasonality.summer: Prime viewing time with peak activity and multiple litters of young. Adults have sleek, shorter summer coats and are frequently seen grazing in open areas during early morning and evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Developing thicker, grayer winter coats and feeding heavily to build fat reserves. Often seen gathering near reliable food sources like gardens and bird feeding areas.
seasonality.winter: Sporting thick, brownish-gray winter coats that provide excellent camouflage against dead vegetation. Most easily spotted against fresh snow, and tracks are clearly visible in snowy conditions.

funFact: Baby cottontails are born completely helpless - blind, deaf, and nearly hairless - but they grow so incredibly fast that they're ready to leave the nest and survive on their own in just three weeks, making them one of nature's speediest developers.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the rare New England cottontail, but eastern cottontails are generally larger with longer ears and lack the distinct black edging between their ears that New England cottontails have. Memory trick: Eastern cottontails are 'extra' - extra common, extra large ears, extra likely to be seen in open areas.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'rabbits,' cottontails are technically different from true rabbits - they're born helpless in shallow nests above ground, while true rabbits are born more developed in underground burrows. This distinction matters little for identification, but explains why cottontail babies seem so vulnerable compared to what people expect from 'rabbits.'
compareHints: Eastern cottontails are significantly more common and adaptable than their rare cousin, the New England cottontail, preferring more open habitats rather than dense early successional forests. Eastern cottontails are also larger overall with proportionally longer ears and tend to be more tolerant of human presence. The key difference is habitat preference - if you see a cottontail in a suburban yard or open field, it's almost certainly an eastern cottontail.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The New England cottontail is extremely similar to the Eastern cottontail, but tends to be slightly grayer overall with a more prominent rusty neck patch.
